summary: Recognisable three-stream recycling unit, but a single featureless box with pasted-on pixel-font labels; reads as a greybox with colour-coded lids.
critique: Silhouette is one rectangular slab (about 1.6 m wide x 1.2 m tall) with three flat stepped lids sitting on top, so it reads as a crate rather than three moulded recycling bins. Real units (Glasdon Nexus 140 trio: 3 x 595 W, 1195 H, 606 D) are three separate, slightly tapered, rounded-corner bodies with a hood containing the aperture, a hinged front door with lock and a recessed plinth. Here the body has no taper, no vertical split between streams, no door seam, no hinges, no lock, no plinth. The apertures are dark rectangles with no visible depth or coloured surround, and they sit on the body face rather than on a hood. Labels are white rectangles with a blocky pixel/bitmap font, which instantly reads as placeholder. The body is black on the front but mid grey on the back/side faces, an inconsistent two-tone with no reason. A thin blue line is visible at the base edge in views 1 and 3 (lid material leaking onto the base or a z-fighting strip). Lids are thick flat slabs with a single step; real lids are domed or raked toward the front. No wear: no scuffs on the lower body, no dirt line at the base, no fading of the coloured plastic.
suggestions: Split the body into three separate moulded units (595 W x 606 D x 1195 H each) with 10-20 mm gaps or a shared back frame; add a 3-5 degree taper (narrower at base) and 40-60 mm corner radii. ~300-500 tris per unit.

Model a raked hood per unit with a real recessed aperture (e.g. 250 x 80 mm, 60 mm deep, dark interior) and a coloured aperture surround/flap in the stream colour (green/blue/grey) instead of colouring only the lid.

Replace the bitmap labels with a proper decal texture: vector sans-serif text plus the standard recycling pictograms (bottle, paper, bin) on stream-coloured panels; place them on the hood or upper door, not floating mid-body.
Add a front door seam (inset 30 mm groove), two hinge knuckles and a small triangular-key lock cylinder per unit; add a 60-80 mm recessed plinth/kick strip at the base.
Make the body one consistent colour (e.g. charcoal albedo ~0.05-0.07, roughness 0.55-0.65 for moulded polyethylene) and fix the blue strip at the base.
Add a wear/dirt mask: darker grime band on the bottom 150 mm, scuffs around the aperture and door edge, slight UV fading on the lids. A shared 512x512 trim/grime texture is enough.

summary: Correct parts (white pole, spring base, yellow flag) but the flag is a noisy crumpled rag and the base has no ground fitting.
critique: Pole height looks right (about 1.5 m) and the black spring section near the base is a nice touch that sells the 'pro spring' variant. The flag is the main problem: it is covered in high-frequency crinkles and jagged edges, so it reads as a wet dishcloth or torn paper rather than a nylon flag. It is also narrower than it is tall and the lower edge is ragged, while a Laws-of-the-Game flag is at least 500 x 500 mm with clean hemmed edges. There is no pole sleeve: the flag appears glued to the side of the pole, with no fabric wrapping round it and no top cap holding it. Flag material is flat unlit-looking yellow with no fabric sheen or translucency. The pole ends abruptly at the ground with a black rubber boot but no ground socket/collar or sleeve flush with the turf. The pole is a uniform white tube with no top cap and no sign of the slight flex or rubber-coating texture of a spring corner post.
suggestions: Rebuild the flag as a clean 500 x 500 mm square (or 450 x 450 if spec dictates) with 2-3 large, low-frequency folds (wavelength ~200-300 mm, amplitude ~30-50 mm) driven by a sine field, not noise. A 6x6 to 10x10 grid (~100-200 tris) is enough; add a vertex-shader wind sway if the engine allows.
Add a sleeve: the flag's pole edge should wrap round the pole as a 25-30 mm tube for the full flag height, plus a small domed top cap (Ø ~35 mm) on the pole.
Hem the free edges: keep them straight, give the cloth a subtle weave normal (tileable 256x256) and roughness ~0.6, slight back-face translucency if the shader supports it.
Add a ground socket: a flush Ø ~60 mm plastic or steel collar ring sitting in the turf, with the rubber spring base visibly entering it.
Optionally offer chequered or club-colour flag variants via texture swap rather than plain yellow.

summary: Convincing full-size goal with a good hexagonal net and right proportions, but clean CG frame and missing net fixings.
critique: Frame proportions read correctly (7.32 x 2.44 m, round tube about 100 mm, angled rear stanchions and a ground bar). The anti-aliased hexagonal net with sag along the top and side panels is the strongest part and reads well at mid distance. What keeps it CG: the frame is a perfect untextured white tube with uniform specular, with no weld seams at the corner joints, no fixings, no ground sockets or collars where the posts meet the turf. The net is attached to nothing: there are no net hooks/clips along the crossbar and posts, no net support bars or elastic ties, and no pegs or ground bar clips holding the bottom of the net to the turf. The net drape is very uniform: real nets bag at the bottom rear, pool slightly on the ground and show tension lines towards each hook. Net cord colour is pure white and perfectly even.
suggestions: Add net hooks/clips every ~300 mm along the back of the crossbar and posts (small instanced C-hooks, ~20 tris each) and pull the net vertices to those points so the net shows small scallops between fixings.

Add ground fixings: a short socket collar (Ø ~110-120 mm, 20 mm proud) at each post base, and net pegs or clips every ~500 mm along the rear ground bar with the bottom net edge lying 50-100 mm on the turf.

Give the frame a subtle material: off-white powder-coat albedo ~0.75-0.8, roughness 0.35-0.45, with a light grime/grass-stain gradient on the bottom 300 mm and faint scuffs on the posts; add weld seams or a fitted corner joint at the crossbar/post junction.
Make the net drape less uniform: deeper bag at the bottom rear, slight tension lines toward each hook, and a small random per-vertex offset; tint the cord slightly off-white with a little variation.

summary: Low-poly red canopy built from stacked faceted rings with cracks in it; reads as a toy umbrella, not a commercial parasol.
critique: The canopy is a thick, faceted dome made of terraced rings, so instead of fabric panels stretched between ribs it looks like a stack of red plates. Real market/café parasols have 8 straight ribs with the fabric drawn tight between them so each panel is slightly concave and the edge is scalloped, plus a hanging valance flap of 150-200 mm around the rim. None of this is present. The shadow shows a ring of speckled light holes, so the canopy mesh has gaps between its ring sections (asset defect, not renderer). The underside shows no ribs, stretchers, runner/hub or crank; the rim edge looks like a thick slab. The pole is a plain thin grey rod with no joint, crank or tilt mechanism; the base is a plain concrete puck, which is plausible but could carry more detail. The red is uniform with flat matte shading and no seams, stitching or fabric texture.
suggestions: Rebuild the canopy as 8 panels: apex at the hub, 8 straight ribs to a rim radius of ~1.35-1.5 m, each panel sagging 20-40 mm toward its centre; cut the rim edge as a scallop between ribs. ~200-400 tris total. Make it single-surface (or two-sided) and watertight so the shadow has no holes.
Add a 150-200 mm valance flap around the rim (8 scalloped strips) and a vented top cap (small second tier) at the apex.
Model the underside: 8 rib tubes (Ø ~12-16 mm), 8 stretchers from a runner on the pole about 0.5 m below the hub, and the hub itself. Low-poly square-section ribs are fine.
Pole: Ø ~38-48 mm aluminium, ~2.3-2.4 m tall, with a mid joint collar and a crank handle; base: keep the concrete or cast-iron weight but add a bevel and a fixing collar.

Material: fabric albedo less saturated (red ~0.45,0.06,0.06 linear), roughness ~0.8, with a canvas weave normal map, panel seam lines and slight fading/soiling on the top surface; optional sponsor print as a decal.

summary: Three red slats on a single T-post with a thin foot plate; reads as a stool or table rather than stadium bench seating.
critique: As a stadium bench-on-bracket seat, the construction is wrong. Real terrace bench seating is a continuous run of slats (extruded aluminium or recycled plastic) carried on cantilever brackets bolted either to the step tread or to the step riser face, spaced ~1.0-1.5 m apart, with seat height ~400-450 mm above the tread. Here a single tall vertical post rises from a tiny flat foot plate with a horizontal arm at the top, so it looks like a pedestal table: seat height also looks too tall relative to the seat (the post is roughly 1.5-2x the slat depth). The slats have odd angled faceted end bevels that read as chiselled shapes rather than rounded extrusions or end caps. The red slats are glossy and uniform; the bracket is a plain flat-shaded bar with no bolts, welds or base plate fixings. There is no back rest and no seat numbering, which most UK stadium benches have. Hard to read scale, as the grass blades look very large around it.
suggestions: Redesign the bracket as a cantilever: a 50x50 or 60x40 mm steel box section (or 8-10 mm plate) bolted to the step riser or tread with a 150x150x10 mm base plate and 2-4 visible bolt heads, angled arm supporting the slats at seat height 420-450 mm.

Present the asset as a module of a continuous run (e.g. 1.5-2 m of slats over one bracket, slats continuing past both ends) so instances tile into a terrace row; seat depth ~300-350 mm with 2-3 slats of ~95-110 mm width and 10-15 mm gaps.
Replace the chiselled end bevels with rounded profile slats (5-10 mm edge radius) and plastic end caps; ~100-200 tris per slat run.

Materials: slat plastic roughness 0.45-0.55 with slight UV fading and scuffing on the top face; bracket galvanised (albedo ~0.55, metallic 1, roughness 0.5) or black powder coat, with a little rust bloom at bolt heads.
Add seat-number plates or painted numbers every ~450-500 mm along the front slat (cheap decal atlas).

summary: Right type and plausible size of anti-vandal welfare cabin with roller shutters and steps, but too clean, with blank pure-black ends and no structural details.
critique: Overall form is believable for a 32 x 10 ft unit (about 9.75 x 3.05 x 2.44 m), and the corrugated white cladding, roller-shutter window boxes, door with blue sign and galvanised steps with handrails all help. Problems: both end walls render as flat near-black panels with no corrugation, no corner posts and no detail, which looks like missing geometry/material (the side-view render makes this obvious). The back long side is plain grey corrugation with no feature at all. The roof is a perfectly flat white slab with no perimeter lip, no corner lifting eyes/castings, no gutter and no downpipe. There are no forklift pockets in the base frame, no visible base frame channel, and the cabin sits on four small feet with nothing else (real cabins stand on timber sleepers or packers). The door has no canopy, frame trim or kickplate; the window shutters are open but the glass has no frame or mullions. No wear at all: real site cabins show rust bleed from fixings, dirt streaks under the roof edge, dirty lower panels and stickers/notices.
suggestions: Fix the end walls: same corrugated cladding as the sides (or flat plate with a cut-in end window for the welfare variant), add 4 corner posts (~150x150 mm) running full height with cast-style corner lifting eyes at the roof corners.
Add the base frame: a 150-200 mm steel channel all round with 2 forklift pockets (~350 x 120 mm) on each long side; seat the cabin on 4-6 timber sleepers or concrete pads.
Roof: add a 50-80 mm upstand lip, a slight crown, a gutter on one long side and a downpipe at one corner.
Door and windows: add a door frame trim (60 mm), kickplate, a small canopy over the door, window frames and a central mullion; consider a closed-shutter variant.

Wear texture: rust streaks under fixings and roof edge, a grime band on the bottom 400 mm, faint green algae on the shaded side, and decals (site safety signs, hire company number). One 1024x1024 atlas shared across cabin variants.
renderer_notes: The ends may be darker partly because they face away from the sun with only sky ambient, but they are also completely flat and untextured, so the asset contributes too.

summary: Correct 20 ft container proportions with corrugated sides, corner castings and door locking bars; lacks markings, roof corrugation and any wear.
critique: Proportions match ISO 668 (about 6.06 x 2.44 x 2.59 m), corrugation is present on the sides and ends, there are corner castings and the door end has 4 vertical locking bars, which is a solid base. What makes it CG: the corrugation is a soft sinusoidal wave rather than the trapezoidal profile of real Corten panels; the roof is completely flat and smooth (real roofs have shallow cross-corrugations and dents with pooling stains); corner castings are plain boxes with no oval apertures; the bottom side rails and forklift pockets are missing; the door has no hinges, handles, cam keepers or seal gasket line, only bars. No markings at all: real containers carry an owner code and number (e.g. ABCU 123456 7), size/type code, CSC plate, max gross/tare stencil and a logo. No wear: no rust at edges and seams, no dents, no faded paint, no dirt.
suggestions: Change the side corrugation to a trapezoidal profile (pitch ~280 mm, depth ~35-45 mm), and add shallow cross-corrugation or a slight sag to the roof panel; can be done with a normal map on a low-poly box if triangle budget is tight (~1-2k tris total).

Corner castings: 178 x 162 x 118 mm blocks with oval holes on the outer faces (normal map or simple inset). Add bottom side rails with 2 forklift pockets (~360 x 115 mm, at 2050 mm centres) on each long side.
Door end: add 4 hinges per door leaf, locking handles with cam keepers at top and bottom of each bar, the rubber seal line around the doors, and the CSC plate.

Decals: owner code and number in white stencil top-right of the doors and on the sides/roof, size-type code (22G1), max gross/tare stencil, and an optional logo variant; use a decal atlas so instances can vary.
Wear: edge rust and rust bleed down from the roof line, dents on the lower side panels, sun fading on the roof, dirty bottom rail. Vary paint colour per instance (blue, maroon, green, grey) via tint.

summary: Stack of plain bevelled cylinders with a capped top; reads as hockey pucks or weights, not tyres.
critique: The tyres are solid low-sided cylinders (visible facets on the silhouette, roughly 16-24 sides) with a chamfer and no tread, sidewall bulge, lettering or bead. Crucially the top tyre is closed with a flat disc and a raised centre boss, so the stack reads as a pile of weight plates or a barrel; a stack of tyres always shows the open centre (bead hole) and the dark inside of the casing. Real tyre cross-section is a rounded torus-like shape with the sidewall curving into the tread shoulder; here the profile is a straight-sided box with a bevel. The material is flat uniform dark grey with no sheen variation, no tread pattern, no dust or mud. The stack is too regular; real stacks are slightly offset and tilted. Proportions: the tyres look more like ~0.6 m diameter by ~0.2 m wide, plausible for car tyres, but with no rim hole they read wrong at any distance.
suggestions: Model each tyre as a lathed profile: outer Ø ~630-650 mm, bead Ø ~410 mm (16 in), section width ~205 mm, with a rounded shoulder and a slightly bulged sidewall. 24-32 radial segments x 10-12 profile points (~600-800 tris per tyre), and leave the centre open so you see into the casing.
Remove the top cap/disc; the top tyre should show its open bead hole and the dark inner liner, possibly with a little water/leaves inside.

Add a tread normal map (a tileable 512x128 block pattern on the crown) and sidewall lettering/rib detail as a radial normal/AO texture; rubber albedo ~0.03-0.04, roughness 0.75-0.9, with lighter grey dust on top surfaces.
Randomise the stack: per-tyre offset of 10-40 mm, tilt of 1-3 degrees, and mixed widths/diameters; offer a 3, 4 and 5-high variant plus a loose leaning tyre for scatter.
Add dirt/mud on the bottom tyre and a slight sun-bleached grey on the uppermost sidewall.
